front:
Name the processes
responsible for the following
phase changes: solid ⇄ gas
back:
Sublimation (s to g)
Deposition (g to s)

front: Define diffusion and state which states of matter it occurs in
back:
• Net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration (down a concentration gradient)
  • Occurs in gases and liquids (solutions)

front: What is an element?
back: An element is a substance made up of only one type of atom.

front:
Elements can be classified into
two groups based on their
properties; what are these
groups?
back: Metals and non-metals

front: What is a compound?
back:
Two or more elements combined chemically in fixed proportions which can
be represented by formulae

front:
Do compounds have the
same properties as their
constituent elements?
back: No, they have different properties.

front:
Do mixtures have the
same chemical properties as their constituent materials?
back:
The constituent materials keep their own chemical
properties, but the mixture may have different chemical properties (e.g.
melting point) as a whole.

front:
What are the five methods to separate mixtures?

Do these involve chemical reactions?
back:
• Filtration
  • evaporation/crystallisation
  • simple distillation
  • fractional
  • distillation
  • chromatography

They do not involve chemical reactions

front: Describe fractional distillation (3 points)
back:
• Separates a mixture of miscible liquids with different boiling points
  • Mixture is heated until it vaporises and rises up a fractionating column (hot at bottom, cool at top)
  • Each liquid condenses at the height matching its boiling point

front: Describe filtration (3 points)
back:
• Separates an insoluble solid from a liquid
  • Mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel
  • Liquid (filtrate) passes through; insoluble solid (residue) is trapped because its particles are too large

front: Describe paper chromatography (3 points)
back:
• Separates a mixture of soluble substances (e.g. dyes/inks) in a solvent
  • Spot mixture on a pencil baseline above the solvent level
  • Solvent rises up the paper, carrying components at different speeds depending on their solubility and attraction to the paper

front: In a paper chromatography experiment, a compound A has an Rf value of 0.85 - what does it tell you about the compound?
back: It has a higher affinity for the solvent than for the paper.

front:
Describe the structure of an
atom
back:
The atom has a small central nucleus (made up of protons and neutrons)
around which there are electrons.

front:
State the relative masses and
relative charges of the proton,
neutron and electron
back:
Proton: mass 1, charge 1
Neutron: mass 1, charge 0
Electron: mass 1/2000, charge -1

front:
Atoms of the same element have
the same number of which particle
in the nucleus?
back: Protons

front:
Where is the majority of
mass of an atom?
back: The nucleus

front:
How does one calculate the
number of neutrons using mass
number and atomic number?
back: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number.

front: What is an isotope? Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties?
back:
• Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons
  • Same chemical properties because they have the same electronic configuration (same outer-shell electrons)

front: Describe the properties of noble gases (Group 0) and their boiling point trend (3 points)
back:
• Colourless, monatomic gases at room temperature with low boiling points
  • Unreactive (inert) — they have a full outer shell of electrons
  • Boiling point increases down the group as atoms get larger / intermolecular forces get stronger

front:
The elements of Group 0
are more commonly known
as…?
back: The noble gases

front: What is the difference in electron shell configuration between elements in the same period?
back: Same number of electron shells, but number of electrons in their outermost shell increases from left to right across the period.

front:
What change in shell
number is seen as one
moves down a group?
back: The number of shells increases

front:
Elements that react to form
positive ions are…?
back: Metals

front: Which elements do not typically form positive ions during chemical reactions?
back: Non-metals (they usually gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons in covalent bonds).

front:
Elements in Group 1 are
known as…?
back: The alkali metals

front:
Elements in Group 7 are
known as…?
back: The halogens

front: Describe ionic bonding (3 points)
back:
• Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
  • Forms positive metal ions and negative non-metal ions
  • Held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions

front: How are ionic compounds held together?
back: They are held together by electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a giant lattice.

front: State and explain the properties of ionic compounds (3 points)
back:
• High melting/boiling points — strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions need lots of energy to overcome
  • Do not conduct when solid — ions are in fixed positions
  • Conduct when molten or aqueous — ions are free to move and carry charge

front:
How are ionic compounds
formed?
back:
Reaction of a metal with a non-metal.
Electron transfer occurs - metal gives away its outer shell electrons to
non-metal.

front: What is a covalent bond?
back: Covalent bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction of a shared pair of electrons of two atoms and their nuclei.

front: Describe the structure and properties of simple molecular covalent substances
back:
- Weak intermolecular forces, so low melting and boiling points
- Small molecules
- Do not conduct electricity (no ions)

front:
How do intermolecular forces
change as the mass/size of the
molecule increases? How does this affect boiling/melting points?
back:
They increase. That causes melting/boiling points to increase as well (more
energy needed to overcome these forces)

front: Describe giant covalent structures: properties & examples (4 points)
back:
• Billions of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice
  • Very high melting/boiling points (many strong covalent bonds to break)
  • Usually do not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons — except graphite)
  • Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (SiO2)

front: Describe the structure and properties of diamond (4 points)
back:
• Each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds (tetrahedral giant lattice)
  • Very hard and very high melting point (many strong covalent bonds)
  • Does not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons)

front: Describe the structure and properties of graphite (4 points)
back:
• Each carbon forms 3 strong covalent bonds in layers of hexagonal rings
  • Soft / slippery — weak intermolecular forces between layers let layers slide
  • High melting point — strong covalent bonds within layers
  • Conducts electricity — 1 delocalised electron per carbon is free to move

front: Describe and explain the properties of fullerenes and give the most common example
back:
– hollow shaped molecules

– based on carbon 6-rings, some 5/7

– C60 (Buckminsterfullerene)

front:
Describe and explain the
properties of nanotubes
back:
– cylindrical fullerene with high length to diameter ratio
- High tensile strength (strong bonds)
- Conductivity (deloc. electrons)

front: What is graphene
back: A single layer of graphite.

front: What affects the energy needed to change state from solid to liquid or liquid to gas?
back: The strength of forces between particles. Stronger forces mean higher energy, melting, and boiling points.

front:
A pure substance will melt
or boil at…? What about the
mixture?
back:
A fixed temperature.
A mixture will melt over a range of temperatures.

front:
What are the three states of
matter?
back: Solid, liquid and gas

front:
Write a balanced equation
of magnesium reacting with
hydrochloric acid.
back: Mg<sub>(s)</sub> + 2HCl<sub>(aq)</sub> → MgCl<sub>2(aq)</sub> + H<sub>2(g)</sub>

front:
The following reaction occurs in a heated test tube:

4MgO(s) + CH4(g) → 4Mg(s) + 2H2O(g) + CO2(g)

The mass appears to decrease. Why?
back: The carbon dioxide and water escape as they are gases

front:
What is the formula that
links mass, molecular mass
and moles together
back: Mass (g) = Mr x Moles

front: Give 3 reasons why actual yield is often less than theoretical yield
back:
• Reversible reaction — may not go to completion
  • Product loss — during transfer, filtration or purification
  • Side reactions — reactants form unwanted by-products

front:
State three characteristics of
the alkali metals
back:
• One electron in their outer shell
  • Low density
  • Very reactive (stored under oil to prevent reactions with oxygen or water)
  • Soft (can be cut with knife).

front:
Describe the product (and its colour) formed by reacting Group 1 elements with non-metals.

Why are these reactions similar for the different Group 1 elements?
back:
The products are soluble white ionic compounds that form colourless solutions.

They all have one electron in their outer shell.

front: How do Group 1 metals react with water, and what are the products?
back:
• React vigorously: fizz, float and move on the surface (potassium burns with a lilac flame)
  • Produce hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide (dissolves to form an alkaline solution)

front: State five characteristics of Group 7 (halogens)
back:
- 7 electrons in outer shell
- Coloured vapours
- Mostly diatomic molecules
- Form ionic salts with metals
- Form molecular compounds with non-metals

front: State the colour and state at room temperature of the halogens (Group 7)
back:
• Fluorine: pale yellow gas · Chlorine: pale green gas
  • Bromine: red-brown liquid (orange vapour)
  • Iodine: grey solid (purple vapour when heated) · Astatine: black solid

front: State three trends seen down group 7 (halogens)
back:
- Higher atomic mass
- Higher melting and boiling point
- Less reactive (electrons less easily gained)

front:
Write the
equation and state the colour change seen when a bromine solution reacts with a sodium iodide solution.
back: Br2(aq)  + 2NaI(aq) → I2(aq)  + 2NaBr(aq); a brown colour of I2 in solution would appear

front: State the solubility rules for common salts (4 rules)
back:
• All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble
  • All nitrates are soluble
  • Chlorides are soluble except silver and lead(II)
  • Sulfates are soluble except barium, calcium and lead(II)

front:
You have a sample of a
pure liquid. What's the simple way to check its identity?
back:
Measure the boiling point.
Say we have water - it boils at 100 Celsius degrees.

front: What is the chemical test for the presence of water?
back:
• Add the liquid to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white)
  • Turns blue (hydrated copper(II) sulfate) if water is present

front: Describe the test for ammonium ions (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) (3 steps)
back:
• Add dilute sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and warm gently
  • Ammonia gas (NH3) is given off
  • Test gas with damp red litmus paper → turns blue

front:
State the colours of flames
observed when lithium,
sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions burn
in oxygen
back:
Red, Li+
Yellow, Na+
Lilac, K+
Orange-red, Ca2+
Blue-green, Cu2+

front:
What is
oxidation/reduction in terms of oxygen?
back:
Oxidation is the addition of oxygen
Reduction is the loss of oxygen

front:
What is oxidation/reduction in terms of
electron transfer ?
back:
Oxidation – loss of electrons.   OIL
Reduction – gain of electrons.  RIG

front:
What is the general equation for a
reaction between metals and
acids? What type of reaction is
this?
back:
Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen
Redox reaction, also a displacement reaction.

front:
Which metals in the reactivity
series will react with acid? What gas is given off?
back: Those above hydrogen. Hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) is given off.

front:
What is the general equation for a
neutralisation reaction?
back: Acid + Base → Salt + Water

front:
What is the general equation for
the reaction between metal
carbonate and acid?
back: Metal Carbonate + Acid → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide

front:
What is the general equation for
the reaction between metal oxide
and acid?
back:
Metal Oxide + Acid → Salt + Water
(Same as alkali + acid)

front: What is a redox reaction?
back: A reaction where both oxidation and reduction occurs

front:
Explain in terms of gain or loss of
electrons which species has been
oxidised and which species has been
reduced when magnesium reacts with
hydrochloric acid
back:
Magnesium has lost electrons and thus has been oxidised (Mg to Mg<sup>2+</sup>)
The hydrogen in HCl has gained electrons and thus has been reduced (H<sup>+</sup> to H<sub>2</sub>)

front:
What do acids and alkalis
produce in aqueous solutions?
back: Acids produce hydrogen ions, alkalis produce hydroxide ions

front:
What is the pH scale and what
does a pH of 7 show?
back: The measure of acidity/alkalinity of a solution; neutral solution.

front:
State the general equation for a
neutralisation reaction in a short,
ionic form.
back:
H<sup>+</sup>
 + OH<sup>−</sup>
 → H<sub>2</sub>O

front: Compare strong acids and weak acids in aqueous solution
back:
• Strong acid: completely ionises (dissociates) in water → higher H+ concentration, lower pH
  • Weak acid: only partially ionises in water → lower H+ concentration, higher pH

front:
What happens to pH as
concentration of H<sup>+</sup>
 increases?
back: It decreases.

front: Compare concentrated vs dilute acids with strong vs weak acids
back:
• Concentrated vs dilute: how many moles of acid are dissolved per unit volume of water
  • Strong vs weak: whether the acid fully or partially ionises in water (at the same concentration, strong acids have lower pH)

front:
Name the following salts:
LiNO<sub>3</sub>
, K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
, MgBr<sub>2</sub>
, BaSO<sub>4</sub>
back:
Lithium nitrate
Potassium carbonate
Magnesium bromide
Barium sulfate

front: State the tests for H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub> (4 gases)
back:
• Hydrogen: lit splint gives a squeaky pop
  • Oxygen: relights a glowing splint
  • Carbon dioxide: turns limewater milky/cloudy
  • Chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper white

front: How is sodium hydroxide used to test for copper and iron?
back:
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate
Iron(II) forms a dirty green precipitate
Iron(III) forms a brown precipitate

front:
Describe the test for
carbonate anions
back:
Add dilute acid, e.g. HCl
Fizzing observed, as CO2 is evolved -> then do limewater test
E.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2

front: Describe the test for sulfate ions (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>)
back:
• Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride (BaCl2) solution
  • Positive result: white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO4)

front: What are the approximate proportions of the top four gases in the modern atmosphere
back:
78% of N2
21% of O2
1% of Argon
0.04% of CO2

front: How have human activities led to an increase in the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane?
back:
Carbon dioxide – combustion of fossil fuels and deforestation.
Methane – increased farming and decomposition in landfills.

front: Give 4 potential effects of global climate change
back:
• Melting glaciers & ice caps → rising sea levels and coastal flooding
  • More extreme weather & changed rainfall patterns
  • Habitat loss and shifts in wildlife distribution
  • Reduced crop yields / water stress in some regions

front: Give 2 problems caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
back:
• Dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain (acidifies lakes, damages plants & limestone buildings)
  • Cause respiratory problems in humans

front: Give four examples of exothermic reaction
back: Freezing, condensing, combustion, oxidation, respiration and neutralisation.

front: Give four examples of endothermic reaction
back: Melting, boiling, thermal decomposition and photosynthesis

front: What is activation energy?
back: Minimum amount of energy that particles need to react.

front:
Name three common ways of
measuring rate of reaction
back:
1. Loss in mass of reactants

2. Volume of gas produced

3. Time for a solution to become opaque (precipitation).

front: How do you measure reaction rate by mass loss? (3 steps)
back:
• Place the reaction flask (with cotton wool plug) on a mass balance
  • Record the decrease in mass at regular time intervals as gas escapes (not suitable for H2 — too light)
  • Plot mass against time; steeper gradient = faster rate

front: Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring the volume of a gas
back:
Connect a gas syringe to a reaction flask and measure the volume of a gas
formed in time intervals. Plot a graph of volume vs time.

front: How do you measure reaction rate using the disappearing cross method?
back:
• Place the reaction flask over a paper marked with a black cross (X)
  • Mix reactants and start a stopwatch
  • Measure the time taken for the precipitate/cloudiness to obscure the cross (rate ∝ 1 ÷ time)

front: How do you find the rate of reaction at a specific time t from a graph?
back:
• Draw a tangent to the curve at time t
  • Calculate the gradient (slope) of the tangent (steeper tangent = faster rate)

front:
State five factors affecting the
rate of a chemical reaction
back:
Concentration of reactants
Pressure of gases (volume)
Surface area
Temperature
Catalysts

front: Describe and explain the effect of increasing concentration on the rate of reaction
back:
- Conc. increases = faster reaction,
- More reactants = more frequent collisions

front: Describe and explain the effect of increasing pressure of a gas on the rate of reaction
back: More gas molecules in the same volume lead to more frequent collisions, increasing the reaction rate. (Similar to increasing concentration)

front: Explain the effect of increasing surface area on reaction rate
back:
• Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface particles
  • Increases the frequency of successful collisions → faster rate
  • Example: magnesium powder reacts faster with acid than a magnesium block

front: How does changing reactant or product concentration shift a reversible equilibrium?
back:
• Increase reactant concentration: equilibrium shifts right → more product formed
  • Decrease product concentration: equilibrium shifts right → more reactants react to replace it

front: What is the empirical formula and how does it relate to the molecular formula?
back:
• Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
  • Molecular formula = empirical formula × a whole-number multiplier (e.g. CH2 × 7 → C7H14)

front:
What is a homologous
series?
back:
Series of compounds with same general formula, same functional groups

similar chemical properties
gradual change in physical properties

front: Hydrocarbon combustion: what kind of reaction and possible products.
back:
An exothermic reaction with oxygen, releasing energy.

Products: water and either carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide/carbon. (depending on oxygen availability)

front: Describe the physical properties and trends of alkanes as chain length increases (3 points)
back:
• Boiling point and viscosity increase (stronger intermolecular forces)
  • Volatility and flammability decrease
  • Generally unreactive (saturated — only single C–C bonds)

front: What is the first step in the fractional distillation of crude oil?
back: Crude oil is heated and vaporised, and the vapour rises up the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.

front:
What type of reaction is
cracking?
back: Thermal decomposition.

front: How are the products of cracking used in polymerisation?
back: Alkanes and alkenes are used as monomers in polymerisation to form plastics and other products

front: What is the test for alkenes?
back: Add bromine water. Colour change occurs from orange to colourless.

front: Compare the combustion of alkanes and alkenes
back:
• Alkanes: burn with a cleaner flame (less soot; mostly CO2 + H2O)
  • Alkenes: burn with a smokier flame (more incomplete combustion / soot due to a higher C:H ratio)

front:
What are addition reactions
of alkenes?
back:
When atoms are added across a carbon-carbon double bond, converting it to a single bond. 

(This reaction increases the saturation of the molecule.)

front: Explain what happens to the double bond when alkenes are used to produce polymers?
back: The C=C double bond becomes a single bond, and the two carbons form bonds to neighbouring monomers.

front:
Give 3 examples of addition
polymers and their uses.
back:
Polyethene - plastic bags

Polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE) - teflon surfaces, for use in non-stick kitchenware

Polychloroethene [previously know as PVC] - water pipes

front:
What is the arrangement of
C-H bonds in methane?
back: Tetrahedral

front:
Why are alkanes considered
unreactive?
back:
They exclusively contain relatively strong C-C and C-H bonds; these are quite
difficult to break.

front: Describe the reaction of alkanes with halogens (3 points)
back:
• Substitution reaction: a halogen atom replaces a hydrogen atom
  • Requires UV light
  • Example: CH4 + Br2 → CH3Br + HBr (or CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl)

front: What are isomers? How many isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> are there?
back:
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
C5H12 has 3 isomers:

front: Addition polymerisation requires an additive - what’s its name and role?
back:
An initiator.

It helps one of the C=C bonds to break, starting the process.

front: Define acid
back: Produces hydrogen ions (H<sup>+</sup>) in aqueous solutions (proton donors) and so have a pH range between 0 and 7

front: Define alkali
back: Alkalis are soluble bases that produce hydroxide ions (OH<sup>-</sup>) in aqueous solutions. They have a pH range between 7 and 14.

front: Define base
back:
A substance which reacts with an acid in a neutralisation reaction to form a salt and
water only. Bases are known as proton acceptors.

front: Define climate change
back:
A change in global climate patterns largely caused by the
increase in concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

front: Describe combustion
back: The burning of a substance in oxygen. Exothermic.

front: Define corrosion
back:
The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the
environment, e.g. rusting occurs when iron is exposed to water and oxygen.

front: Define displacement reaction
back: A chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from a compound.

front: How do you carry out a flame test? (3 steps)
back:
• Identifies metal ions (cations)
  • Clean a nichrome/platinum wire loop in concentrated HCl and dip into the sample
  • Hold in a roaring blue Bunsen flame and observe the flame colour

front: Define galvanise
back: A process used to protect against corrosion by coating the metal with a protective layer of zinc.

front: Describe the greenhouse effect
back:
The increase in the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere due to the
greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trapping infrared radiation emitted from the surface.

front: Define halides
back: The ions formed when halogen atoms gain an electron. E.g. Cl<sup>-</sup>,  Br<sup>-</sup> and I<sup>-</sup>

front: Define indicators and give 3 examples
back:
A substance used to distinguish between acidic and alkaline solutions.

Examples include phenolphthalein, litmus and methyl orange.

front: Define neutralisation
back: The reaction in which an acid and a base (including alkalis) react to form a salt and water.

front: Define pH scale
back:
A measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution ranging from 0 to 14. The pH
can be measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.

front: Define reactivity series
back: A series in which metals are arranged in order of their reactivity. This can be used to predict products from reactions.

front: Define reducing agent
back:
A substance that brings about reduction by losing electrons. The reducing
agent is itself oxidised.

front: Define reduction
back: A reaction involving the loss of oxygen. Reduction is the gain of electrons.

front: What is rust and what causes it?
back: iron oxide which forms on iron when it undergoes oxidation - in the presence of oxygen and water

front: Explain how sacrificial protection prevents iron from rusting (3 points)
back:
• Attach or coat iron with a more reactive metal (e.g. zinc or magnesium)
  • The more reactive metal loses electrons (oxidises) more easily than iron
  • It corrodes instead of the iron — even if the coating is scratched

front: Define thermal decomposition
back: The breaking down of a compound by heating

front: Define universial indicator
back: A mixture of dyes that changes colour gradually over a range of pH and is used in testing for acids and alkalis.

front: Define atomic nucleus
back:
Positively charged object composed of protons and neutrons at the centre
of every atom with one or more electrons orbiting it.

front: Define atomic number
back: The number of protons in the nucleus.

front: Define conductor
back:
A material that contains charged particles which are free to move to carry
electrical or thermal energy.

front: Describe crystallisation (3 steps)
back:
Separates a soluble solid from a solution:
  • Heat gently to evaporate some water until a saturated solution forms (crystals appear at the edge)
  • Leave to cool so crystals form
  • Filter off the crystals and pat dry with filter paper

front: Define electron
back:
Negatively charged subatomic particle which orbits the nucleus at various energy
levels. Very small relative mass (negligible).

front: Define electron shell
back: Different energy levels in atoms, occupied by electrons.

front: Define electrostatic forces
back: The strong forces of attraction or repulsion between charged ions

front: Define empirical formula
back:
The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a
compound.

front: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in a gas (3 points)
back:
• Far apart and randomly arranged
  • Move rapidly and randomly in all directions
  • Highest kinetic energy; very weak forces between particles

front: Define group
back: A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in the outer shell.

front: What does inert mean?
back: Unreactive.

front: What are intermolecular forces, and what property do they affect?
back:
The forces which exist between molecules.

The strength of the intermolecular forces impact physical properties like boiling/melting point.

front: Define ion
back: An atom or molecule with an electric charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.

front: Describe lattices - what do they form?
back: A repeating regular arrangement of atoms/ions/molecules that occurs in crystals.

front: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid (3 points)
back:
• Close together in a random/irregular arrangement
  • Can slide / move past each other
  • Moderate forces of attraction between particles

front: Define mass number
back: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

front: Define metals
back:
Elements that react to form positive ions. Found to the left and towards the bottom of
the periodic table.

front: Define mixture. Comment on their boiling/melting points.
back:
Contains at least two different elements or compounds which are not chemically bonded together.

They may melt or boil over a range of temperatures.

front: Define mobile phase
back:
The fluid (gas or liquid) which moves through the chromatography system,
carrying the mixture which is to be separated.

front: Define mole
back:
Standard unit for measuring amounts of chemicals. The mole is the unit for amount of
substance. The symbol for the unit mole is mol.

front: Define molecular formula
back: The actual ratio of atoms of each element present in a compound.

front: Define molecule
back: A group of at least two atoms held together by covalent bonds.

front: Describe noble gases
back:
The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table. They have a stable full outer
shell of electrons which makes them very unreactive.

front: Define neutron
back: Neutral subatomic particle present in the nucleus of the atom. Relative mass of 1.

front: Define non-metals
back:
Elements that react to form negative ions. Found towards the right and top of
the periodic table.

front: Define percentage yield
back:
Ratio of actual product obtained to the theoretical maximum, as a percentage:
Percentage yield = actual yieldtheoretical yield × 100

front: Define period with reference to electron shells
back: A row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.

front: What is the periodic table?
back:
Table of elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number and such
that elements with similar properties are in the same column (group).

front: Define proton
back:
Positively charged subatomic particle present in the nucleus of the atom. Relative
mass of 1.

front: Define pure substance
back: A substance which contains only one compound or element and so has fixed melting and boiling points.

front: Define relative atomic mass
back:
An average value that takes account of the abundance of the
isotopes of the element.

front: Define relative formula mass.
back:
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers
shown in the formula

front: Define saturated solution
back:
A solution which contains the maximum amount of solute that can be
dissolved in the solvent. If any more solute is added, it will not dissolve in the solution.

front: Describe simple distillation (3 points)
back:
Separates a pure liquid (solvent) from a solution:
  • Heat the solution so the solvent evaporates / boils
  • Vapour passes into a cold condenser and condenses back into liquid
  • Pure liquid is collected as the distillate

front: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in a solid (3 points)
back:
• Regular arrangement, tightly packed together
  • Vibrate about fixed positions only
  • Least kinetic energy; strong forces between particles

front: Define solute
back: A substance which is dissolved in a solvent to create a solution.

front: Define solution
back: A homogeneous mixture in which a solute is dissolved in a solvent.

front: Define solvent
back: A substance which dissolves a solute.

front: Define state symbols
back:
The symbols used in chemical equations to denote the states of the
chemicals reacting: (s) - solid, (l) - liquid, (g) - gas, (aq) - aqueous solution.

front: Define stationary phase
back:
The nonmoving phase which the mobile phase passes over during
chromatography.

front: Define subatomic particles
back:
Particles smaller than an atom. Protons, neutrons and electrons are
the three most common subatomic particles.

front: Define water crystalisation
back: Water molecules forming part of a crystal structure.

front: Define activation energy
back: The minimum amount of energy that particles must collide with to react.

front: Define calorimetry
back:
The process used to measure the amount of heat energy released or absorbed
during a chemical reaction.

front: Define catalyst
back:
Increases the rate of reaction by providing a different reaction pathway with a lower
activation energy. They are not used up during the reaction.

front: According to collision theory, what is required for a reaction to happen?
back:
Chemical reactions only occur when colliding particles collide with the
correct orientation and with sufficient energy (activation energy).

front: Explain in terms of collisions why increasing surface area increases reaction rate
back:
• More reacting particles are exposed at the surface
  • More frequent successful collisions → higher rate of reaction

front: Explain in terms of collisions why increasing temperature increases reaction rate (3 points)
back:
• Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster → more frequent collisions
  • A greater proportion of particles have energy ≥ the activation energy
  • Many more frequent successful collisions → faster rate

front: Define endothermic reaction
back:
A reaction in which energy is taken in from the surroundings so the
temperature of the surroundings decreases.

front: Define enthalpy change
back: The amount of heat energy given out or absorbed during a reaction.

front: Define exothermic reaction
back:
A reaction in which energy is transferred to the surroundings so the
temperature of the surroundings increases.

front: Define molar enthalpy change (ΔH) and how to calculate it (3 points)
back:
• Heat energy released or absorbed per 1 mole of substance reacted
  • Formula: ΔH = Q ÷ moles (in kJ/mol)
  • Sign: negative (−) for exothermic, positive (+) for endothermic

front: Define rate of reaction (including units)
back:
The measure of the amount of product formed or reactant used over time.
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s, cm<sup>3</sup>/s or mol/s.

front: Define reversible reaction
back:
A reaction in which the products can react together to reform the
reactants. Reversible reactions are denoted by the symbol ⇌.

front: Define addition polymerisation
back:
The reaction in which many small molecule monomers bond
together to form a long chain polymer.

front: Define addition reaction
back:
A reaction in which at least two molecules combine together to form a
single larger product.

front: Define alkanes, including the general formula
back:
The most common hydrocarbon found in crude oil. Alkanes have the general
formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>.

front: Define alkenes, including the general formula
back:
Hydrocarbons with a double bond between two of the carbon atoms in their chain (C=C),
causing them to be unsaturated. They have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>.

front: Define biodegradable
back: Able to be broken down by living organisms.

front: What is catalytic cracking (incl conditions)
back: Long-chain hydrocarbons are heated to 600-700°C, turning to gas. The vapour passes over a catalyst, splitting the molecules.

front: Define complete combustion
back:
Combustion carried out in sufficient oxygen. Water and carbon
dioxide are the only products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.

front: Define cracking
back:
A process that involves breaking down larger hydrocarbons to produce smaller
more useful molecules.

front: What is crude oil? (3 points)
back:
• A finite fossil fuel found in rocks
  • Formed from ancient plankton / marine biomass buried under mud over millions of years
  • A mixture of hydrocarbons (mostly alkanes)

front: Define displayed formula
back:
A type of structural formula that shows all the bonds between every
atom in the compound.

front: Define finite resource
back: A resource which will one day run out, e.g. crude oil.

front: Define fuel
back: A substance which releases energy when burned

front: Define general formula and give an example
back:
• An algebraic formula that applies to every member of a homologous series
  • Example: alkanes = CnH2n+2 (where n = number of carbon atoms)

front: Define hydrocarbons
back: Compounds made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

front: What are impurities? Give an example of an issue with combustion.
back:
Substances within a compound different to compound itself.
E.g. combustion of hydrocarbons continuing sulfur impurities leads to the formation of sulfur dioxide.

front: Define incomplete combustion
back:
Combustion which is carried out with insufficient oxygen. It can
lead to the production of toxic carbon monoxide and carbon particulates.

front: Define isomerism
back:
The existence of molecules with exactly the same molecular formula but a
different arrangement of atoms in space

front: Define monomer
back: Small short chain molecules which can join together to form a long chain polymer.

front: What do particulates come from and why are they bad?
back:
Carbon particulates (soot) are a product of incomplete combustion. They cause global dimming and health problems for
humans.

front: Define polymer
back: Large long-chain molecules made up of lots of small monomers joined together by covalent bonds.

front: Define saturated hydrocarbons
back:
A hydrocarbon compound containing only single bonds between
carbon atoms. Alkanes are saturated compounds.

front: Define structural formula
back:
A formula which shows the arrangement of atoms in the molecule of a
compound but does not show all the bonds between them. E.g. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>.

front: Define substitution reaction
back:
A reaction in which a functional group of a compound is replaced by
another functional group.

front: Define unsaturated compounds
back:
A compound that contains double or triple carbon bonds so
that it does not contain the maximum number of hydrogen atoms. Alkenes are unsaturated
compounds.

front: What is the formula for R<sub>f</sub>?
back:
Rf = distance moved by spot (solute)distance moved by solvent front
(Always between 0 and 1 — no units)

front: What is the general formula for the reaction between a metal and water?
back: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen

front: What are the colours for litmus paper?
back: AcidicRedNeutralPurpleAlkalineBlue

front: What are the colours for phenolphthalein?
back: Acidic / NeutralColourlessAlkalinePink

front: What are the colours of methyl orange?
back: AcidicRedNeutralOrangeAlkalineYellow

front: How do you test for halides?
back:
Add dilute nitric acid (HNO3), then silver nitrate solution (AgNO3):
Chloride (Cl⁻)White ppt (AgCl)Bromide (Br⁻)Cream ppt (AgBr)Iodide (I⁻)Yellow ppt (AgI)
  • Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)
  • Ag+(aq) + Br−(aq) → AgBr(s)
  • Ag+(aq) + I−(aq) → AgI(s)

front: What are refinery gases used for?
back: Domestic heating and cooking

front: What is gasoline used for?
back: Fuel in cars

front: What is kerosene used for?
back: Fuel in aircraft

front: What is diesel used for?
back: Fuel in some cars, larger vehicles and trains

front: What is fuel oil used for?
back: Fuel for large ships and some power stations

front: What is bitumen used for?
back: To surface roads and roofs

front: What is the general formula for the combustion of a hydrocarbon?
back:
hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
(Complete combustion in plentiful oxygen)

front: Write the equation and state the colour change seen when a chlorine solution reacts with a sodium bromide solution.
back:
Cl2(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → Br2(aq)  + 2NaCl(aq)

in this reaction, an orange colour of Br2 in solution would appear

front: Name the commonly insoluble ionic compounds
back:
Common carbonates - all insoluble, except potassium, sodium and ammonium

Common hydroxides - all insoluble, except potassium, sodium and calcium

front: How does a fractionating column separate crude oil? (3 points)
back:
• Crude oil is heated until it vaporises and enters a column that is hot at the bottom, cool at the top
  • Long-chain hydrocarbons (high boiling points) condense near the bottom
  • Short-chain hydrocarbons (low boiling points) rise and condense near the top

front: Draw the displayed formula for the reaction of ethene (C2H4) with bromine (Br2).
back: Addition reaction — a bromine atom adds across the C=C double bond to form 1,2-dibromoethane (orange bromine water turns colourless):

front: What is the relationship between alkalis and bases?
back:
Alkalis are a subset of bases that are soluble in water.

All alkalis are bases. Not all bases are alkalis.

front: What is physical chemistry?
back: The study of how substances react, focusing on energy, rates of reaction, and molecular interactions

front: What is organic chemistry?
back: The study of carbon-containing compounds and their reactions.

front: What is inorganic chemistry?
back: The study of non-carbon compounds, including metals and salts.

front: What does soluble mean?
back: A substance is soluble if it can be dissolved in a solvent, e.g. salt in water. An insoluble substance won’t dissolve in a particular solvent.

front: What is the link between relative formula mass and moles
back: Relative formula mass of a substance is numerically equal to the mass of one mole of the substance in grams

front: What information can you read from a paper chromatogram? (3 points)
back:
• 1 spot = pure substance; 2 or more spots = mixture
  • Spots at the same height (same Rf value) indicate the same substance
  • A spot that stays on the baseline is insoluble in that solvent

front: Core practical: give 3 key precautions when setting up paper chromatography
back:
• Draw the baseline in pencil (graphite is insoluble so it won’t run up the paper)
  • Keep the solvent level below the pencil line so spots don’t dissolve directly into the solvent
  • Cover the beaker with a lid to prevent volatile solvent evaporating; mark the solvent front before drying

front: State the formula linking moles, mass and relative formula mass (Mr)
back:
moles = mass (g)Mr (or Ar)
  • Rearranged: mass = moles × Mr
  • Mr = sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of all atoms in the formula

front: What are the 3 steps to calculate a reacting mass from a balanced equation?
back:
• Step 1: find moles of the known substance (moles = mass ÷ Mr)
  • Step 2: use the molar ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of the unknown
  • Step 3: convert back to mass (mass = moles × Mr)

front: How do you calculate empirical formula and then molecular formula from data? (3 steps)
back:
• Step 1: divide the mass (or %) of each element by its Ar to get moles
  • Step 2: divide every mole value by the smallest → simplest whole-number ratio (empirical formula)
  • Step 3: multiplier = Mr ÷ empirical formula mass; multiply empirical subscripts by this number

front: Core practical: how do you determine the formula of magnesium oxide by combustion? (4 points)
back:
• Weigh crucible + lid, add coiled magnesium and reweigh
  • Heat strongly, lifting the lid briefly to let O2 in without letting white MgO smoke escape
  • Heat to constant mass so all Mg has completely reacted
  • Mass of O = mass of MgO − mass of Mg → convert both masses to moles (÷ Ar) for the ratio

front: How do you write the formula of an ionic compound from its ions?
back:
• Balance the ion numbers so total positive charge = total negative charge (overall neutral)
  • Use brackets if you need more than one compound ion (e.g. Mg2+ + 2 OH− → Mg(OH)2; 2 NH4+ + SO42− → (NH4)2SO4)

front: What are the 3 rules for drawing an ionic dot-and-cross diagram?
back:
• Show outer-shell electrons using dots for one element and crosses for the other
  • Metal atom loses outer electrons; non-metal gains them to achieve a full outer shell
  • Put square brackets around each ion with its charge outside top-right (e.g. [Mg]2+)

front: Define a covalent bond in terms of electrostatic attraction
back: • A strong electrostatic attraction between the positively charged nuclei of two non-metal atoms and the shared pair(s) of negatively charged electrons between them

front: How many covalent bonds do H, halogens, O, N and C normally form in dot-and-cross diagrams?
back:
• H & halogens (Group 7): 1 bond (e.g. H2, HCl, Cl2)
  • Oxygen: 2 bonds (H2O has 2 singles; O2 has 1 double bond)
  • Nitrogen: 3 bonds (NH3 has 3 singles; N2 has 1 triple bond)
  • Carbon: 4 bonds (CH4 4 singles; CO2 two double bonds; C2H4 one C=C double bond)

front: Why do covalent compounds not usually conduct electricity?
back:
• Covalent molecules are electrically neutral (no overall charge)
  • They have no free-moving ions and no delocalised electrons to carry charge (exception: graphite)

front: How do reactions of Li, Na and K with water show the Group 1 reactivity trend? (3 points)
back:
• Reactivity increases down Group 1 (Li < Na < K)
  • Evidence: Li fizzes steadily; Na melts into a ball and fizzes faster; K ignites immediately with a lilac flame
  • Outer electron is further from the nucleus (more shells/shielding) → weaker attraction → lost more easily

front: How do colour, melting/boiling point and reactivity change going down Group 7 (halogens)?
back:
Going down Group 7 (F → Cl → Br → I → At):
  • Colour gets darker (pale yellow → pale green → red-brown → grey → black)
  • Melting & boiling points increase (gas → liquid → solid)
  • Reactivity decreases (outer shell further from nucleus → harder to gain an electron)

front: How do iron or phosphorus experiments determine the percentage of oxygen in air?
back:
• Wet iron filings (rusting) or heated phosphorus reacts with all the O2 in a trapped volume of air
  • The gas volume decreases by about 21% (water rises up the tube)
  • % O2 = (decrease in volume ÷ initial volume of air) × 100

front: Core practical: give 3 precautions when finding the % of oxygen in air
back:
• Use an excess of iron/copper/phosphorus so all the oxygen reacts
  • Ensure the apparatus is completely airtight
  • Allow the apparatus to cool back to room temperature before measuring the final gas volume

front: State the Reactivity Series of metals from most reactive to least reactive
back: Potassium > Sodium > Lithium > Calcium > Magnesium > Aluminium > (Carbon) > Zinc > Iron > (Hydrogen) > Copper > Silver > Gold

front: Core practical: how do you compare the reactivity of Mg, Zn, Fe and Cu with dilute acid?
back:
• Add equal masses/surface areas of each metal to equal volumes & concentrations of dilute HCl or H2SO4
  • Compare rate of fizzing (H2) and temperature rise
  • Order: Mg (vigorous) > Zn (steady) > Fe (slow) > Cu (no reaction)

front: Define an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer
back:
• Acid: a proton (H+) donor
  • Base: a proton (H+) acceptor

front: What types of substance act as bases, and how is an alkali different?
back:
• Bases: substances that neutralise acids — metal oxides, metal hydroxides, and ammonia
  • Alkalis: soluble bases that dissolve in water to produce OH− ions

front: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base (4 steps)
back:
• Warm the dilute acid and add excess insoluble base (until solid remains, ensuring all acid reacts)
  • Filter to remove the excess unreacted solid
  • Heat gently to evaporate some water until saturated (crystals start forming)
  • Leave to cool to crystallise, filter off crystals, and pat dry with filter paper

front: Core practical: how do you make pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals?
back:
• Warm dilute sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and add excess black copper(II) oxide (CuO) while stirring
  • Filter out excess black CuO to obtain a clear blue CuSO4 solution
  • Evaporate some water over a water bath/gentle flame, then cool to form blue crystals
  • Filter off crystals and pat dry between filter papers

front: What is the physical test to show a sample of water is pure?
back:
• Measure its boiling point (pure water boils sharply at 100 °C) or melting/freezing point (0 °C)
  • Impurities raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point

front: State the equation for heat energy change (Q) and define every symbol
back:
Q = m c ΔT
  • Q = heat energy transferred (J)
  • m = mass of water/solution heated (g; 1 cm3 = 1 g)
  • c = specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J/(g °C))
  • ΔT = temperature change (°C)

front: Core practical: how do you reduce errors when measuring temperature changes (calorimetry)? (3 points)
back:
• Solutions (dissolving/neutralisation/displacement): use an insulated polystyrene cup + lid inside a beaker and stir continuously
  • Combustion (spirit burner): use a draught shield and stir the water in a copper can
  • Main source of error: heat loss to the surroundings (and incomplete combustion)

front: Core practical: how do you investigate different solid catalysts on H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> decomposition? (3 points)
back:
• Add equal masses of different solids (e.g. MnO2, CuO) to equal volumes/concentrations of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)
  • Measure the volume of O2 collected in a gas syringe in a fixed time (fastest = best catalyst)
  • Filter, dry and reweigh the solid to confirm its mass is unchanged

front: Describe the 2 specification examples of reversible reactions
back:
• Hydrated copper(II) sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous CuSO4 (white) + water (heat → white; add water → blue + gets hot)
  • Ammonium chloride (white solid) ⇌ ammonia (NH3) + hydrogen chloride (HCl) (heat decomposes; cooling reforms white solid)

front: State the IUPAC prefixes for 1–6 carbons and endings for alkanes & alkenes
back:
• 1 C: meth- · 2 C: eth- · 3 C: prop- · 4 C: but- · 5 C: pent- · 6 C: hex-
  • -ane: alkane (single bonds) · -ene: alkene (C=C double bond; number gives lowest position, e.g. but-1-ene)
  • Halogens use prefixes: chloro-, bromo- (e.g. 1,2-dibromoethane)

front: Distinguish between molecular, structural and displayed formulae (plus isomers)
back:
• Molecular: actual numbers of each atom (e.g. C4H10)
  • Structural: atoms grouped carbon-by-carbon (e.g. CH3CH2CH2CH3)
  • Displayed: draws every atom and every covalent bond
  • Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formula

front: Why is carbon monoxide (CO) poisonous? (2 points)
back:
• CO binds strongly (irreversibly) to haemoglobin in red blood cells
  • Reduces the blood’s capacity to carry oxygen around the body (can cause suffocation/death)

front: How are oxides of nitrogen formed in car engines?
back:
• Very high temperatures inside car engines provide enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react together
  • Forms oxides of nitrogen (NOx), which contribute to acid rain

front: Why is cracking necessary in the oil industry? (2 points)
back:
• Crude oil has a surplus of long-chain hydrocarbons (low demand, thick/viscous) and a shortage of short-chain alkanes (high demand for petrol/fuels)
  • Cracking also produces alkenes, needed as raw materials for making polymers

front: What is the functional group of alkenes?
back:
• A carbon–carbon double covalent bond (>C=C<)
  • Makes alkenes unsaturated and more reactive than alkanes

front: Name the alkenes with 2, 3 and 4 carbons (including the two unbranched butene isomers)
back:
• 2 C: ethene (CH2=CH2)
  • 3 C: propene (CH2=CHCH3)
  • 4 C (unbranched isomers): but-1-ene (CH2=CHCH2CH3) and but-2-ene (CH3CH=CHCH3)

front: How do you convert between an alkene monomer and its addition polymer repeat unit?
back:
• Monomer → repeat unit: change C=C to a C–C single bond, draw two trailing bonds extending through brackets, add subscript n
  • Repeat unit → monomer: remove brackets & trailing bonds and restore the C=C double bond

front: Core practical: how do you investigate surface area and acid concentration using marble chips and dilute HCl? (4 points)
back:
• React calcium carbonate (marble chips) + dilute HCl → CO2 gas
  • Measure rate by volume of CO2 (gas syringe / upturned cylinder) or mass loss on a balance at regular time intervals
  • Surface area: compare equal masses of large vs small marble chips (same acid volume, concentration & temperature)
  • Concentration: vary HCl concentration (same mass/size of marble chips & temperature) → smaller chips / higher concentration give steeper initial gradient
